title: Arriving at Bucknell and playing in Diffy's orchestra
summary: At Bucknell he joined Diffendaffer's dance band for the fraternity dance circuit, playing fox trots, waltzes and light classics.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: What steps did you take next?
My next step was I went away to college at Bucknell University.

Lewisburg, Pennsylvania, and I played with an orchestra there and there was a chap there, a trombone player that I had played with the summer previous. He was from around Wilkes Barre and when I got there, and saw him, I heard he was there, I looked him up -- oh, he said, 'Come around and play with the band and join the fraternity and all that sort of thing.

But they worked every weekend. Friday and Saturday nights. The school had -- it was a coeducational school and they had lots of fraternities. The ladies had their fraternities, and the men they had theirs. So they would space out their dances and it was a small school. There weren't any more than 800 people at the time I got there -- so it's a lot bigger now.

They would space their dances out so that the boys could have the girlfriends and the girlfriends could have the boyfriends and they would go to a dance almost every week or weekend throughout the year, when they could get the band and this fellow, a fellow by the name of Diffendaffer. Diffy they called him. Diffy's orchestra, and we had two banjos. Banjo was rhythm, ukelele, very popular then and we had two banjos and then he had a saxophone player and I went down and played along-side of him.

But it wasn't very long before they had formed another orchestra. There was plenty of work around and we then had the two banjos, piano, drums and a trombone and a saxophone. And that was quite a combination, but everything then was melodic, play the popular tunes of the day, no blues, just -- there were no -- nothing more than that, play fox trots all the time and sometimes a fast one. The one-step was very popular then, if you could get it in.
Around the college they wanted pretty much a little beat and a little fox trot rhythm and waltzes.

No, we had maybe one or two there that liked the Charleston or the Black Bottom, we would play it, but nobody seemed to be interested in that, you know, the way it came out and the way the records came out, everything was Charleston, every bar was Charleston. The whole thing, it got

monotonous and the band that we had, we played strictly for college crowd. We didn't go out -- very seldom would we go out to a dance hall. So that we had actually the cream of the listening crowd. The enthusiasm was great, when you play a fraternity dance and they all go and a lot of the same ones go to each one, throughout the year. I think they were allowed four in each one.
It doesn't take long for you to practically know everybody there and they come around to hear the music and to dance to it, if they like. We were popular there.

But other things that we used to play there too at the time were things like --- (SINGS) da, ded, ("Song of India" -- ed) Tommy made a record of that. I can't give it out. Well, (figure) to a Wild Rose, " for example, (inaudible) .
Right. " My Heart at Thy Sweet Voice."

Those were very popular with the band and they were well received by your dancing public, because what, it was nice smooth melody. You could get a nice, for a fox trot, you could wind up with a nice walk. And now we haven't mentioned trumpet, haven't got into the trumpet.
